text: Sarv Mittra Sikri (26 April 1908 – 24 September 1992) was an Indian lawyer and judge who served as the 13th Chief Justice of India.[1] He previously held the position of the first Advocate-General for Punjab and was the first judge of the Supreme Court of India to be directly appointed from the Bar; he is one of only two judges to have become CJI directly from the Bar.[2] Born in Lahore on 26 April 1908,[3] Sikri moved to London to study medicine but switched to law, studying at Trinity College, Cambridge.[1] Before returning to Lahore in 1930, he served as a barrister-at-law at Lincoln's Inn in London. He began his legal practice in the chambers of Jagannath Agarwal, a leading advocate in the Lahore High Court who specialized in criminal and civil law. After independence, he was appointed Assistant Advocate General of Punjab in 1949 and became the Advocate General in 1951, holding that position almost continuously until his elevation to the Supreme Court of India in 1964.[4] As an advocate, he appeared and practised in various courts, including the Lahore High Court, other courts in Punjab, the Federal Court of India, and eventually the Supreme Court of India.[5] In the case of I.C. Golaknath and Ors. v. State of Punjab and Anrs., Sikri was part of a 6:5 minority that reversed the court's earlier decision upholding Parliament's power to amend all parts of the Constitution, including Part III on Fundamental Rights, thereby effectively removing Parliament's power to curtail Fundamental Rights.[4] This Indian law–related biographical article is a stub.
